provisioning:The Monday market on the Ri.name: Monday market on the Riera
provisioning:The Monday market on the Ri.teaser: Once a week the dry riverbed that serves as the village car park fills with stalls instead
provisioning:The Monday market on the Ri.story: The Riera de Sant Vicenç is a torrent bed that splits Cadaqués in two and runs with water only in storms; the rest of the time it carries the traffic into town and holds the parked cars. On Monday mornings part of it becomes the weekly market, about forty stalls by one count, selling local produce alongside clothes and household goods. It is a working village market rather than a food hall: come for fruit, vegetables, cheese and charcuterie for the galley, and leave the anchovies and the wine to the producers on the next cards.
provisioning:The Monday market on the Ri.why: Provision early on a Monday, then walk a few steps up the same riverbed to Compartir for lunch (its own card is in the tables).

provisioning:The anchovy salters of L'Es.name: The anchovy salters of L'Escala
provisioning:The anchovy salters of L'Es.teaser: Forty kilometres down the coast, two family houses still fillet salted anchovies by hand
provisioning:The anchovy salters of L'Es.story: L'Escala, about forty kilometres south of Cadaqués, has salted fish since Greek traders landed at Empúries in the 6th century BC, and in 1697 it finished the Alfolí de la Sal, its warehouse for the salt. Two family firms keep the trade: Fills de J. Callol i Serrats, founded 1847 and the oldest in town, and Solés, from 1888. The anchovies come in on the spring run, roughly March to June, sit packed in salt for months and are then filleted by hand. At Callol i Serrats you phone ahead and are walked through the salting before a tasting with local wine; Solés runs a factory-museum with an audioguide.
provisioning:The anchovy salters of L'Es.why: Buy the 'Anxoves de l'Escala' at the source: hand-filleted anchovy is the one thing worth spending on for the galley here.
facts: L'Escala, about 40 km south of Cadaqués; Callol i Serrats on the Carretera d'Orriols, km 20.9

provisioning:Empordàlia.name: Empordàlia
provisioning:Empordàlia.teaser: A farmers' co-op at Pau that presses argudell olives and bottles the Empordà's sweet Garnatxa
provisioning:Empordàlia.story: In 2005 the village co-ops of Pau (founded 1961) and Vilajuïga (1947) merged into Empordàlia, and the old Pau cooperative building on the Roses road became its headquarters, olive mill and farm shop. The oil is Oli de Pau, an extra-virgin pressed from two local varieties, argudell and corivell, off roughly 500 hectares of old groves on the slopes behind the bay of Roses. The cellar makes DO Empordà wines, among them a sweet Garnatxa de l'Empordà. The tour walks the winery and the mill, then pours four wines beside the oil with a plate of local products.
provisioning:Empordàlia.why: Taste Oli de Pau next to the wines and fill the galley with both at the farm shop on the way back from Roses.

provisioning:Martín Faixó.name: Martín Faixó
provisioning:Martín Faixó.teaser: The one winery with vines on the cape itself: slate, tramuntana, and a view down to the bay
provisioning:Martín Faixó.story: Rafa Martín and Carme Faixó opened Can Rafa on the Passeig in the early 1980s (sources say 1981 or 1982); in 2000 the family planted vines at Mas Sa Perafita, on the slate hill above the road into Cadaqués and inside the Cap de Creus natural park. The first wines came in 2007, made by their daughter Ester. Garnatxa, Cabernet, Merlot, Picapoll and Muscat of Alexandria grow on wind-scoured slopes, sold as Perafita and Cadac. For twenty years the family fought for permits to dig an underground cellar into the hill; Ara reported in October 2025 that building would begin in 2026.
provisioning:Martín Faixó.why: Taste the Perafita white on the hill where it grows, then order it at Can Rafa (its own card is in the tables).

provisioning:Mas Estela.name: Mas Estela
provisioning:Mas Estela.teaser: A biodynamic farm in the valley above El Port de la Selva, with wine aged in clay amphorae
provisioning:Mas Estela.story: In 1989 Núria and Diego Soto-Dalmau bought an old farmhouse and about 50 hectares in the Sant Romà valley above La Selva de Mar, inside the Cap de Creus natural park, and farmed it organically from the first season; since 1999 it has been run on biodynamic lines. Their son Dídac now works the estate with them. The vines sit among scrub, stone and old terraces. The range runs from Vinya Selva de Mar and Quindals, some of it aged in clay amphorae, to two sweet wines, Moscatell Estela and Estela Dolç, the second in the old Empordà vi dolç tradition.
provisioning:Mas Estela.why: Ask to taste the Estela Dolç, the Empordà's sweet Garnatxa, poured in the valley where it is made.
facts: Sant Romà valley, La Selva de Mar (17489), above El Port de la Selva

provisioning:Espelt.name: Espelt
provisioning:Espelt.teaser: Vilajuïga's large family estate, and the place to learn the Lledoner grape that runs through the DO
provisioning:Espelt.story: Espelt is one of the largest estates in the DO Empordà, with vineyards spread across the Alt Empordà and its cellar and shop at Mas Espelt, outside Vilajuïga at the foot of the Rodes range. The grapes are the old varieties of this corner of Catalonia: Garnatxa, Carinyena and Lledoner, the local name for the Garnatxa family, whose pink-skinned form makes a Lledoner rosat. The long visit, about two and a half hours, walks what a tourism listing calls the first organic vineyards in Vilajuïga before the tasting, in Catalan, Spanish, English or French.
provisioning:Espelt.why: Taste the Lledoner rosat beside a Carinyena red to understand the whole appellation in one glass each.
facts: Visits by appointment only, about 2.5 h
Lledoner rosat, Garnatxa and Carinyena reds

walks:Camí de Ronda to Cala Nans.name: Camí de Ronda to Cala Nans
walks:Camí de Ronda to Cala Nans.teaser: Round the bay's south shore, past the last white house, to an 1874 lighthouse and its swimming ledges
walks:Camí de Ronda to Cala Nans.story: From the south end of the village the coast path picks its way round Punta des Baluard, the Port de l'Alguer and Punta d'en Pampa, then past Sa Conca, until the houses give out and the way is grey schist, thyme and the slap of swell in the gullies. At the end stands the small Cala Nans light, first lit on 1 September 1874 to bring ships into Cadaqués harbour; its lamp sits 36 m above the sea and carries eight nautical miles. There is no beach, only rock ledges below the lighthouse to swim from, and nothing at all between you and the tramuntana.
walks:Camí de Ronda to Cala Nans.why: Swim off the schist under the light and look back across the bay at the whole of Cadaqués.

walks:Up to Sant Sebastià.name: Up to Sant Sebastià
walks:Up to Sant Sebastià.teaser: A thyme-and-rosemary climb to a hermitage that hangs over the whole bay
walks:Up to Sant Sebastià.story: The path leaves the village and works up the eastern flank of the Pení through thyme, rosemary and rockrose, the scrub releasing its smell as the sun warms it. At about 385 m it reaches the 18th-century hermitage of Sant Sebastià, privately owned since 1890 and opened to the village every 20 January for the saint's aplec, with sardanes and the start of the sea-urchin season. From its terrace the bay, its coves and the Cala Nans light lie underfoot. Do not push on for the summit: the top of the Pení carries a military radar station and is closed to the public.
walks:Up to Sant Sebastià.why: Climb on a clear, cool morning for the long view from the bay of Roses to the Pyrenees.

walks:The Camí Antic to Cap de Creus.name: The Camí Antic to Cap de Creus
walks:The Camí Antic to Cap de Creus.teaser: Cove to cove from Portlligat to the cape, through dead vineyard terraces, the lighthouse ahead all the way
walks:The Camí Antic to Cap de Creus.story: From the AE-252 junction on Portlligat beach the old path crosses the road to Cala Es Jonquet and Platja de Sant Lluís, reaches the shingle of Guillola, then turns uphill on the Camí Antic proper. Here it climbs through dry-stone terraces built by hand against the slope, where Garnatxa and Carinyena vines once grew; sage, thyme and olive trees hold the walls now. Yellow paint marks the way, and the white Cap de Creus lighthouse stays on the skyline the whole time, standing on the easternmost point of mainland Spain. In spring the terraces turn yellow and white with broom and rockrose.
walks:The Camí Antic to Cap de Creus.why: Go in autumn, when the terraces are empty; the summer shuttle has stopped, so plan to walk back or arrange a car at the cape.
facts: About 5.5 km one way; about 14.8 km return from Cadaqués
About 2h20 one way; about 4 h return from Cadaqués

Morning start, to reach the cape before midday; spring for the flowers; clear days for the Pyrenees

Water, sun cover and a windproof layer

walks:The lighthouse and Cala Culip.name: The lighthouse and Cala Culip
walks:The lighthouse and Cala Culip.teaser: From the cape car park down to a shingle cove where a Roman oil ship sank in the 70s AD
walks:The lighthouse and Cala Culip.story: Ten minutes down a slope path from the lighthouse car park lies Cala Culip, fifteen metres of shingle and rock tucked out of the tramuntana. In 1984 divers mapping the cape's seabed found a wreck here: Culip IV, a Roman merchantman that went down in the 70s AD carrying some 79 amphorae of Andalusian olive oil and red sigillata tableware from La Graufesenque in Gaul. It was excavated until 1988; today the snorkel shows sponges, starfish and the odd moray among the rocks. Climb back by the Paratge de Tudela circuit, about 4 km in all, looking down on Cala Jugadora and Cala Fredosa.
walks:The lighthouse and Cala Culip.why: Swim in one of the few cape coves that stays calm when the north wind is blowing.
facts: Cap de Creus lighthouse car park, about 8 km and 20 min by road from Cadaqués; the summer car restriction and its shuttle are over for the year (check the Parc Natural)

walks:GR-92 to El Port de la Selva.name: GR-92 to El Port de la Selva
walks:GR-92 to El Port de la Selva.teaser: The coast path leaves the sea and crosses the bare spine of the peninsula to the next bay north
walks:GR-92 to El Port de la Selva.story: The GR-92 follows the whole Catalan coast, from Portbou on the French border to Ulldecona at the far south, and between Cadaqués and El Port de la Selva it turns its back on the water. The stage climbs inland on stony tracks across the Cap de Creus natural park: bare schist, scrub bent flat by the wind, dry-stone walls and wide views over both bays. El Port de la Selva's tourist office puts it at about three hours, with a steep first fifty minutes from their end. On a longer circuit, the monastery of Sant Pere de Rodes and Sant Salvador de Verdera are within reach.
walks:GR-92 to El Port de la Selva.why: Walk it north, eat on El Port de la Selva's harbour, and arrange a lift back over the hill.
facts: Cadaqués, following the red-and-white GR-92 marks north

calas:Platja Gran.name: Platja Gran
calas:Platja Gran.teaser: The village's own beach: coarse sand over pebbles, with the whole white seafront at your back
calas:Platja Gran.story: Platja Gran is where Cadaqués meets the water: about 200 metres of coarse sand over pebbles straight off the seafront promenade in the centre, the white houses and the bell tower of Santa Maria rising behind it. Small boats are pulled up along it, the entry is easy, and in July and August it is the busiest stretch of shore in the village. It faces the open bay, so when the tramuntana blows the chop rolls straight in. By mid-October the towels have mostly gone and the water is cooling, but a calm morning still makes for a swim with the village as backdrop.
calas:Platja Gran.why: Swim at first light, then take breakfast on the seafront without moving the car.
facts: In the centre, straight off the seafront promenade; no car needed
Early morning; skip it on tramuntana days, when the chop comes straight in
Sea shoes for the pebbles under the sand
The view back up to Santa Maria from the water (the church is its own card)

calas:Es Sortell.name: Es Sortell
calas:Es Sortell.teaser: A stone footbridge out to a pine-topped islet, and the best look back at the white village
calas:Es Sortell.story: About a kilometre south of the centre, out on the Punta de Sa Conca, Es Sortell is a 50-metre cove of grey gravel and rock with a stone footbridge running out to its islet, where pines grow straight out of cracks in the schist. The water is shallow and usually calm, made for a slow swim, and from the islet the whole of Cadaqués stacks up white across the bay. On the way in you pass Es Sortell d'en Ter, a tiny pocket between the rocks with houses all round it. Sa Conca lies just beyond, behind the point.
calas:Es Sortell.why: Cross the footbridge late in the day and watch the village change colour across the water.
facts: On foot about 1 km south of the centre along the shore; parking roughly 300 m above
Late afternoon, for the light on the village
Sea shoes for the gravel and rock

calas:Sa Conca.name: Sa Conca
calas:Sa Conca.teaser: The last beach on the bay's south shore: deep water a few strokes out, and a path on to Cala Nans
calas:Sa Conca.story: Sa Conca sits behind the Es Sortell point at the far south of the village, a half-moon of coarse sand and pebbles about 90 to 100 metres long, with a rocky seabed that drops away so quickly you are out of your depth within a few strokes. It has a long nudist tradition, and the Festival Internacional de Música de Cadaqués has used it as an open-air stage for free concerts (the festival is its own card). From the back of the beach a path carries on round the headland to the Cala Nans lighthouse, which makes it the natural swim stop on that walk.
calas:Sa Conca.why: Fifteen minutes on foot from the centre buys you clear, deep water and far fewer people than Platja Gran.
facts: On foot 15-20 min south along the shore from the centre, or by car to a small lot above
A calm day; in season, check the festival programme for a concert evening

calas:Portlligat beach.name: Portlligat beach
calas:Portlligat beach.teaser: Grey shingle, moored fishing boats and still water in front of Dalí's house
calas:Portlligat beach.story: Over the hill north of Cadaqués, Portlligat is an almost closed bay, so still on a calm morning that it looks like a lake. The beach is 170 metres of grey shingle and cobble, with no sand at all, and the water in front of it is crowded with moored fishing boats. It faces east across that sheltered water, and the house Dalí made here stands just behind the shore (the Casa-Museu card tells its story). The Camí Antic to the cape starts from a junction on this beach, so it is the obvious swim at either end of that walk.
calas:Portlligat beach.why: Swim out between the moored boats in water that stays flat when the rest of the coast is choppy.
facts: On foot 15-20 min over the hill from the centre, or 5 min by car with parking by the bay
Early morning, when the bay is glassy
Sea shoes: it is all shingle

calas:S'Alqueria Gran.name: S'Alqueria Gran
calas:S'Alqueria Gran.teaser: Pebbles, scrub and clear water two kilometres out on the cape road, with nothing laid on
calas:S'Alqueria Gran.story: Two kilometres out along the road to the Cap de Creus lighthouse, a short walk down through dense scrub and rock brings you to S'Alqueria Gran, about 60 metres of pebbles and coarse sand at the back of the Racó des Mor bay. There are no services and no proper car park, which keeps it quiet; the water is clear, and the regulars have long swum without costumes. It makes an easy swim on the drive back from the lighthouse. In mid-October, with the summer shuttle over, you can drive out again; park only where the road allows it.
calas:S'Alqueria Gran.why: Bring everything you need: here there is only water, pebbles and rock.
facts: By car about 2 km along the Cap de Creus lighthouse road, then a short walk down; no dedicated parking
Water, shade and sea shoes; there are no services

calas:Cala Jugadora.name: Cala Jugadora
calas:Cala Jugadora.teaser: A pocket of sand right under the cape lighthouse, with seagrass meadows to snorkel
calas:Cala Jugadora.story: Right under the Cap de Creus lighthouse, about 7 km north of the village, Cala Jugadora is a 15-metre pocket of coarse sand and gravel reached by a ten-minute path down the slope. It is sheltered from the tramuntana, so it can be flat when the cape above is roaring. Put your face in the water and the seabed is a patchwork of rock, tongues of sand and meadows of Posidonia, the seagrass that keeps this water clear and hides the small fish. It fills fast in summer for exactly that reason; mid-October, with the crowds gone and the sea still holding some warmth, suits it well.
calas:Cala Jugadora.why: Snorkel the Posidonia, then climb to Restaurant Cap de Creus by the lighthouse (in the tables).
facts: By car to the Cap de Creus lighthouse, then 10 min down a slope path; the summer car restriction is over for the year (check the Parc Natural)
A tramuntana day, when it stays sheltered while the cape blows
